proposals.label: Croci et al. (2022)
proposals.rationale: Croci et al. (2022) report a new homozygous MEGF10 missense mutation, c.2096G-C (p.Cys699Ser), which is not in the variant table, in an Italian man born to consanguineous parents. Unlike the mild nonprogressive course already recorded, his disease began early and progressed slowly. He had dysphagia, global areflexia, rhinolalia and hyperlordosis, and his later biopsy showed myofibrillar changes (whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions). Based on this case, the authors proposed that MEGF10-related phenotypes form a continuum.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man, born to healthy consanguineous parents, with a congenital myopathy. From the first months of life he had weak suction, elbow contractures and scoliosis. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation and needed resuscitation for asphyxia. Motor development and intellect were normal. He then developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia and respiratory involvement, and from age 16 years he needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy, cleft palate, global areflexia, contractures of the elbows and ankles, and hyperlordosis. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, and cardiac studies were normal. A first muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions and minicores. Electrophysiologic studies were normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential. The authors proposed that the minicores seen in the late-onset group may result from longstanding myofibrillar pathology that begins in infancy.

proposals.label: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021)
proposals.rationale: The paper adds a new homozygous MEGF10 splice-site mutation, c.2980+5G>C, found in a consanguineous Saudi family with the mild phenotype. This variant is not in the variant table, and RT-PCR showed that it causes retention of 85 bp of intron 23. The paper also widens the mild phenotype: it adds areflexia, spinal rigidity, mild oral dysphagia, normal CK, neurogenic EMG, and an affected sister who died at 18 months.

paragraphs.text: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) reported a boy (patient 2) with a mild form of MEGF10-related congenital myopathy. His parents were first cousins in a consanguineous Saudi family. Fetal movements had been decreased during the pregnancy, and he had generalized hypotonia from the newborn period. He had feeding difficulties, choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and motor delay. He sat at 21 months, and at age 9 years he walked independently, though he ran slowly. He had no major cognitive deficits and did not need long-term oxygen. On examination he had plagiocephaly, facial diplegia, a high-arched palate, low-set ears, and mild thoracic scoliosis with spinal rigidity. He also had axial-predominant hypotonia, proximal weakness, a positive Gowers sign, areflexia, and joint hyperlaxity. Creatine kinase and nerve conduction were normal. EMG showed neurogenic changes, and a modified barium study showed mild oral dysphagia. A sister with a similar phenotype died at 18 months of respiratory infections.

evidence.statement: AlMuhaizea et al. (2021) reported a boy (patient 2) from a consanguineous Saudi family (parents were first cousins) with a mild form of MEGF10-related congenital myopathy. He had generalized hypotonia from the newborn period, after a pregnancy with decreased fetal movements. He had feeding difficulties, choking, recurrent aspiration pneumonia and motor delay, but he sat at 21 months and was walking independently, though running slowly, at age 9 years. He had no major cognitive deficits and did not need long-term oxygen. On examination he had plagiocephaly, facial diplegia, a high-arched palate, low-set ears, mild thoracic scoliosis with spinal rigidity, axial-predominant hypotonia, proximal weakness, a positive Gowers sign, areflexia and joint hyperlaxity. Creatine kinase was normal, nerve conduction was normal, EMG showed neurogenic changes, and a modified barium study showed mild oral dysphagia. A sister with a similar phenotype died at 18 months of respiratory infections.
quotes: A four-year-old boy from a consanguineous Saudi family (first-degree cousins) presented with neonatal-onset generalized hypotonia. The pregnancy was complicated by decreased fetal movements. He had one sister with a similar phenotype who passed away at the age of 18 months with respiratory infections.

His last clinical follow up was at the age of 9 years when he was noted to be walking independently, but was a slow runner. He was able to draw a line and completely undress himself. He engaged in-group play and had no major cognitive deficits. He did not require long-term oxygen support.
He had a positive Gower sign but no calf muscle hypertrophy. His deep tendon reflexes were absent. He also had joint hyperlaxity of knees, wrists, and elbows.

proposals.label: Li et al. (2021)
proposals.rationale: The entry's only animal model is the zebrafish morphant. Li et al. (2021) add the first Megf10-null mouse data, showing impaired satellite cell activation and migration and reduced regeneration with fibrosis after repeated injury. This is mechanistic support for the satellite cell hypothesis already in the entry.

paragraphs.text: Li et al. (2021) studied Megf10-null mice. In single myofibers isolated from extensor digitorum longus muscles and cultured for 24, 48, and 72 hours, fewer satellite cells detached from Megf10-null myofibers than from wildtype myofibers. Fewer Pax7+/MyoD+ activated satellite cells were associated with Megf10-null myofibers, and these cells migrated shorter distances. Satellite cells that detached from Megf10-null myofibers also had fewer MyoD-positive nuclei. The authors concluded that Megf10 contributes to an early stage of satellite cell activation, during which the cells migrate to target myofibers. To deplete the satellite cell pool, Li et al. (2021) gave 3 sequential intramuscular barium chloride injections into the tibialis anterior muscle, starting at 2 months of age. Compared with wildtype muscle, injured Megf10-null muscle showed significantly reduced regeneration, with pockets of atrophic fibers, clusters of small myofibers with internalized nuclei, greater variability in fiber size, and more fibrosis on fibronectin staining.

proposals.rationale: Saha et al. (2019) add the first therapeutic evidence: SSRIs, especially sertraline, relieved abnormalities in several MEGF10-deficient models. paragraphs.text: Saha et al. (2019) ran a small-molecule screen in Megf10-deficient myoblasts and identified 2 selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), sertraline and escitalopram. They followed up in Megf10 -/- mouse myoblasts, in myoblasts derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of patients with MEGF10 myopathy, in Drosophila deficient in the MEGF10 homolog Drpr, and in megf10 mutant zebrafish. Sertraline was highly effective at relieving abnormalities in all of these models and restored Notch1 deficiencies. The authors concluded that SSRIs, especially sertraline, show promise as therapies for MEGF10 myopathy, and they suggested that the mechanism may involve the Notch pathway.

proposals.label: Draper et al. (2019)
proposals.rationale: Draper et al. (2019) report a Drosophila gain-of-function (overexpression) model of mouse Megf10 and its fly homolog Draper. Overexpression caused lethality through somatic muscle, at late stages of myogenesis, and selectively damaged tubular muscle. It also produced wing phenotypes resembling reduced Notch signaling. The disorder is recessive loss-of-function, so this overexpression model bears only indirectly on its mechanism and belongs more in the gene entry. It is a minor addition to the existing zebrafish morpholino data.

paragraphs.text: Draper et al. (2019) studied gain of function of Megf10 in Drosophila. Ubiquitous overexpression of mouse Megf10 or of Drosophila Draper (Drpr) isoforms I, II, or III caused a nearly universal failure to eclose. Flies developed normally until metamorphosis, then arrested, and many died at the dark pupa/pharate adult stage. The few escapers had abnormal legs and wings, including darkened tibia/tarsus junctions and absent tarsal segments, which were reminiscent of Drpr-deficient flies. Muscle-targeted overexpression with the How-Gal4 driver reproduced the lethality. Expression in tendon, heart, glia, neurons, motor neurons, intestinal tract/malpighian tubules, and fat body was well tolerated. Overexpression was tolerated in adult muscle precursors, muscle progenitor and founder cells, terminally differentiated fibers, and mature adult muscle. It was lethal with the Mef2-Gal4 (differentiation) and apterous-Gal4 (muscle identity) drivers. The authors concluded that overexpression is harmful at stages of myogenesis later than the stage sensitive to Drpr deficiency. The effect was muscle subtype selective. Drivers marking precursors of tubular muscles (apterous-Gal4, cut-Gal4) caused lethality, whereas a driver marking precursors of fibrillar indirect flight muscles (vestigial-Gal4) yielded viable adults. Draper et al. (2019) examined 12 escaper Wg-Gal4>UAS-drpr-III adults at 2 days of age. In 8 of the 12, the tubular jump muscle fibers showed enlargement, hyalinization, abnormal localization or loss of nuclei, loss of striations, and disrupted bundle organization. Fibrillar indirect flight muscle was spared, and none of 15 control flies had abnormalities. Overexpression in Notch-positive or Wingless-positive wing disc cells caused arrest at the dark pupal/pharate adult stage. Overexpression in cells expressing Serrate produced a split-vein phenotype at the wing margin that resembled decreased Notch signaling. This phenotype was fully penetrant with the short isoforms Drpr-II and Drpr-III and about 50% penetrant with Drpr-I. Drpr-II also caused a held-out wing phenotype and markedly reduced locomotor activity.

paragraphs.text: Draper et al. (2019) postulated that at least one conserved extracellular domain mediates the lethality of overexpression by compromising normal interactions with protein partners. The candidate domains were those present in the shortest isoform, Drpr-III: the EMI domain, a DSL (Delta/Serrate/LAG-2)-like domain, or the 4 EGF-like domains. They also suggested that Megf10/Drpr and Notch may interact to regulate myogenesis. Among the conserved C-terminal tyrosine residues, they noted that MEGF10 Y1030 appeared most closely associated with EMARDD, because defective phosphorylation at this residue had been linked to pathogenic mutations.

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) found that ubiquitous overexpression of mouse Megf10 or of Drosophila Draper (Drpr) isoforms I, II, and III each caused a nearly universal failure to eclose; the flies developed normally until metamorphosis and then became arrested, with many dying at the dark pupa/pharate adult stage. The few escapers had structural abnormalities of the legs and wings, including darkened tibia/tarsus junctions and absent tarsal segments, reminiscent of Drpr-deficient flies.
quotes: Ubiquitous overexpression of Drpr isoforms I, II, III and mouse Megf10 in the w1118 wildtype fly background each leads to a nearly universal failure to eclose (Fig. 1), suggesting that the motif responsible for the lethality is to be found in all isoforms of Drpr, including the shortest one, Drpr-III.

We observed that flies that overexpress Megf10 or Drpr develop normally until metamorphosis then become arrested, while control siblings proceed to the adult stage (Fig. 2). Many Megf10- overexpressing flies reach the dark pupae/pharate adult stage where they die (Fig. 2).
Strikingly the observed leg abnormalities, including darkened tibia/tarsus junctions and absent tarsal segments, are reminiscent of those seen in Drpr-deficient mutant flies (Supplementary Fig. 1).

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) reported that the lethal phenotype was reproduced by overexpression of mouse Megf10, Drpr-I, or Drpr-II in muscle with the How-Gal4 driver, whereas targeted expression to tendon, heart, glial cells, neurons, motor neurons, intestinal tract/malpighian tubules, and fat body was well tolerated. The authors concluded that the damaging effects of Megf10/Drpr overexpression in Drosophila are related to somatic muscle.
quotes: The lethality phenotype is reproduced with overexpression of mouse Megf10, Drpr-I or Drpr-II in muscle, using the How-Gal4 driver.

Similarly, targeted expression of Megf10/Drpr to the heart, glial cells, neurons, motor neurons, intestinal tract/malpighian tubules and fat body with corresponding drivers is well-tolerated (Table 1 and Fig. 3).

The current studies suggest that the mechanisms underlying Megf10/Drpr overexpression-induced damaging effects in Drosophila are related to somatic muscle, as only ubiquitous and muscle-specific overexpression led to lethality, whereas overexpression in multiple other tissues (including the tendons, heart, glia, neurons) was tolerated.

evidence.statement: Using stage-specific Gal4 drivers, Draper et al. (2019) showed that Megf10/Drpr overexpression in adult muscle precursors (twist-Gal4), muscle progenitor and founder cells (kirre-Gal4), terminally differentiated fibers (Mhc-Gal4), and mature adult muscle (DJ757, DJ667) was well tolerated, whereas overexpression with the Mef2-Gal4 (differentiation) and apterous-Gal4 (muscle identity) drivers was lethal. The authors concluded that Megf10/Drpr overexpression is harmful at stages of myogenesis later than the stage sensitive to Megf10/Drpr deficiency.
quotes: Targeted Megf10/Drpr overexpression to the AMPs/muscle precursor cells (using the twist-Gal4 driver), as well as to muscle progenitor and founder cells (using the kirre-Gal4 driver), is well tolerated.
In contrast, lethality is observed when using the Mef2-Gal4 (Mef2 induces differentiation) and apterous-Gal4 (apterous is a muscle identity gene) drivers (Table 1 and Fig. 4).
These results indicate that Megf10/Drpr overexpression is harmful at specific stages of myogenesis that occur later than the stage that is sensitive to Megf10/Drpr deficiency.

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) found that the detrimental effect of Megf10/Drpr overexpression was muscle subtype selective: crosses with the apterous-Gal4 or cut-Gal4 drivers, which mark myoblasts giving rise to tubular muscles (direct flight muscles and jump/leg muscles), led to lethality, whereas crosses with the vestigial-Gal4 driver, marking precursors of the fibrillar indirect flight muscles, yielded viable adults.
quotes: While crosses established with either apterous-Gal4 or cut-Gal4 lead to lethality in the experimental progeny, crosses with vestigial-Gal4 result in the generation of viable adults (Table 1, Fig. 5).

Apterous (ap) and cut (ct) promote the development of tubular muscles that compose the direct flight muscles (DFMs) and jump/leg muscles, while vestigial (vg) positive fibers develop into the fibrillar indirect flight muscles (IFMs) (Fig. 5).

We show that transgene-induced Megf10/Drpr expression is well-tolerated in the developing IFM/ fibrillar fibers (using the vestigial-Gal4 driver), but is lethal in the developing DFMs/ tubular fibers (using the Ap-Gal4, or cut-Gal4, driver).

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) reported that histologic analysis (H&E) of 2-day-old Wg-Gal4>UAS-drpr-III adult flies that escaped lethality showed marked abnormalities of the tubular fibers of the tergal depressor of the trochanter (jump muscle), including fiber enlargement, hyalinization, abnormal localization or loss of nuclei, loss of striations, and disruption of bundle organization, in 8 of 12 flies, while fibrillar indirect flight muscle fibers were spared and 15 control flies showed no abnormalities.
quotes: Notably, H&E staining of tissues from wgG4>Drpr-III adult flies that escape lethality show clear abnormalities in the tubular fibers that comprise the jump muscle, but not in the fibrillar fibers of the indirect flight muscles (Fig. 8, Supplementary Fig. 2).

The defects include marked enlargement of the fibers, hyalinization, abnormal localization/loss of nuclei, loss of striations and disruption of the characteristic bundle organization. In contrast to the tubular muscles, no gross abnormalities are detected in fibrillar fibers that comprise the large indirect flight muscles
N = 12 flies. Of note, 8 out of 12 flies where tubular fibers could be observed displayed abnormalities.

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) found that overexpression of Drpr-I, Drpr-II, Drpr-III, or Megf10 in Notch-positive wing disc cells caused death at the dark pupal/pharate adult stage, and that overexpression of Drpr-II in Wingless-positive cells likewise caused developmental arrest at that stage, with escapers of the other isoforms being short-lived.
quotes: Increased expression of Drpr-I, Drpr-II, Drpr-III or Megf10 in Notch positive cells of the wing disc results death of the flies at the dark pupal/pharate adult stage (Fig. 7A and7E).

In addition, increased expression of Drpr-II in Wingless (Wg)-positive cells also leads to developmental arrest at the dark pupal/pharate adult stage (Fig. 7A). Although some progeny that overexpress Megf10 or the other Drpr isoforms (i.e., Drpr-I, Drpr-III) in Wg cells can escape lethality, these flies are short-lived (data not shown).

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) showed that overexpression of Drpr in wing cells expressing the Notch ligand Serrate produced a split-vein (extra-branching) phenotype at the wing margin similar to that of decreased Notch signaling, fully penetrant with the short Drpr-II and Drpr-III isoforms and about 50% penetrant with Drpr-I; Drpr-II additionally caused a held-out wing phenotype and markedly reduced locomotor activity compared with controls.
quotes: Targeting increased expression of Drpr in selected wing cells that express the Notch ligand Serrate (using the Serrate-Gal4 driver) results in a split vein (extra-branching) phenotype at the wing margin (SerG4>Drpr, Fig. 7A-C), similar to that seen in flies with decreased Notch signaling activity.
The phenotype is 100% penetrant when overexpressing the short Drpr-II and Drpr-III isoforms, and moderately penetrant (~50%) when overexpressing the longer Drpr-I protein.
In addition, SerG4>Drpr II flies display markedly reduced locomotor activity versus corresponding controls that do not express the Drpr-II transgene (Fig. 7D, Supplementary video).

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) noted that Drpr is the Drosophila homolog of human MEGF10, MEGF11, and MEGF12 (Jedi), and sequence alignment of Drpr isoforms I-III with mouse Megf10 and Megf12/Jedi showed high conservation of the extracellular EMI domain, a Delta/Serrate/LAG-2 (DSL)-like domain characteristic of Notch ligands, and four distal EGF-like/laminin-like domains; a Delta and OSM-11 (DOS)-like motif was present in the longest members (Drpr-I, Megf10, Jedi) but not in Drpr-II or Drpr-III, and the intracellular NPXY motif was conserved.

evidence.statement: Draper et al. (2019) postulated that at least one conserved extracellular domain present in the shortest isoform Drpr-III (EMI, DSL, or the four EGF-like domains) mediates the overexpression lethality by compromising normal interactions with protein partners, and that Megf10/Drpr and Notch may interact to regulate myogenesis, with Notch and Drpr playing divergent roles in delineating myoblast identity toward indirect versus direct flight muscle fibers.
quotes: We postulate that at least one of the conserved extracellular domains present in the shortest isoform Drpr-III (i.e. EMI, DSL, four EGF-like domains), plays a major role in inducing fly lethality (when overexpressed in muscle) by compromising normal interactions with protein partners.
Complementary genetic analyses show that Megf10/Drpr and Notch may interact to regulate myogenesis.
In the developing IFM and DFM muscle fibers, we thus found that Notch and Drpr play divergent roles and function to delineate myoblast identity toward one muscle type or the other.

(2019) stated that MEGF10 myopathy, also known as EMARDD (early onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress and dysphagia), is a rare human congenital muscle disease caused by recessive mutations in MEGF10, which encodes a single transmembrane receptor expressed in skeletal muscle, retina, and CNS glial cells.
quotes: Recessive mutations in multiple epidermal growth factor-like domains 10 (MEGF10) underlie a rare congenital muscle disease known as MEGF10 myopathy.

MEGF10 myopathy or EMARDD (Early onset Myopathy, Areflexia, Respiratory Distress and Dysphagia) is a rare human congenital muscle disease caused by mutations in multiple EGF-like domains 10 (MEGF10). This single transmembrane receptor is expressed in skeletal muscles, the retina and in CNS glial cells, and is conserved through evolution.
